issues.legal_issue: A tenancy of premises governed by rent-control legislation is extinguished when the building let to the tenant is completely destroyed by an accidental natural event.
material_facts: The tenant had rented a shop, not the land beneath it, and the tenancy was governed by the state rent-control legislation.
An accidental fire completely destroyed the shop, leaving only vacant land; the landlord had not demolished the building.
The tenant erected a new shop on the site without the landlord’s consent or permission.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy in the destroyed shop was extinguished. The tenant could not rely on the general property-law provision concerning destruction to continue occupying the vacant land or to claim a right to occupy a replacement building.
issues.legal_principle: A lease requires an existing subject matter; when the building alone was let and it is completely destroyed, the tenancy ends. The general option under Section 108(B)(e) of the Transfer of Property Act does not give a tenant of premises governed by a special rent-control statute a right to remain on the vacant site after total destruction. The special statute regulates buildings, not vacant land: the definition in Section 2(1) does not make the land beneath a building part of the building merely because a structure once stood there. Sections 108(B)(e) and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, read with the special nature of the rent-control scheme, support this result. The Court relied on V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, Pradesh Kumar Bajpai v. Binod Behari Sarkar, K.K. Krishnan v. M.K. Vijaya Ragavan and Prithvichand Ramchand Sablok v. S.Y. Shinde concerning the special statute’s displacement of inconsistent rights under the Transfer of Property Act. It agreed with the approach in George v. Varghese, Thomas v. Moram Mar Baselious Ougen and Siddharthan v. Ramadasan, and rejected the contrary views in Hind Rubber Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. Tayebhai Mohammedbhai Bagasarwalla and V. Kalpakam Amma v. Muthurama Iyer Muthurkrishna Iyer. The result would differ if the landlord himself demolished a building, in which case the rent-control statute’s reconstruction provisions would apply.

rule.if: tenancy_dispute_after_total_destruction and premises_let_as_building_only and rent_control_scheme_applies and building_completely_destroyed_by_accident and not landlord_demolished_building

predicates.tenancy_dispute_after_total_destruction: The dispute concerns whether a tenancy continues after the rented premises have been completely destroyed.
predicates.premises_let_as_building_only: The landlord let a building or premises, rather than the land beneath it, to the tenant.
predicates.rent_control_scheme_applies: The tenancy was governed by a special rent-control scheme regulating the rented building.
predicates.building_completely_destroyed_by_acciden: An accidental event completely destroyed the rented building, leaving no building for the tenant to occupy.
predicates.landlord_demolished_building: The landlord demolished the rented building.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns a tenancy of a building governed by rent control, and the building is completely destroyed accidentally rather than demolished by the landlord, the tenancy is extinguished.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court has jurisdiction over a landlord’s suit to recover vacant land after the rented building governed by rent-control legislation has been completely destroyed.
material_facts: The landlord sued for possession of the land after the rented shop was completely destroyed by accidental fire.
The rent-control legislation governed the shop, not the vacant land left after its destruction.
No building remained, and the rent-control legislation did not provide a ground for eviction based on destruction of the building or a remedy to recover the vacant site under that legislation.
issues.conclusion: The civil court was competent to entertain and try the suit for recovery of possession of the vacant land.
issues.legal_principle: The rent-control statute protects occupation of a building and does not regulate vacant land. Where the rented building has been completely destroyed and no superstructure remains, the statute provides no remedy for recovering possession of the vacant site; the landlord may therefore seek possession through a civil suit. The Court considered Section 11 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, which provides grounds for eviction from premises governed by that Act, together with its conclusion under Section 2(1) that the Act concerns buildings rather than vacant land. Its discussion of V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, Pradesh Kumar Bajpai v. Binod Behari Sarkar, K.K. Krishnan v. M.K. Vijaya Ragavan and Prithvichand Ramchand Sablok v. S.Y. Shinde recognizes the special statute’s role in matters it governs; it does not extend that role to recovery of a bare site outside its scope.

rule.if: civil_suit_for_vacant_land_possession and rented_building_completely_destroyed and no_superstructure_remains and rent_control_scheme_covers_buildings_not_vacant_land and rent_control_scheme_lacks_vacant_site_recovery_remedy

predicates.civil_suit_for_vacant_land_possession: A landlord brought a civil suit seeking possession of the vacant land on which a rented building had stood.
predicates.rented_building_completely_destroyed: The building rented to the tenant was completely destroyed.
predicates.no_superstructure_remains: No building or other superstructure remains on the site.
predicates.rent_control_scheme_covers_buildings_not: The applicable rent-control scheme governs buildings and does not govern vacant land alone.
predicates.rent_control_scheme_lacks_vacant_site_re: The applicable rent-control scheme provides no remedy for recovering possession of the vacant site after the rented building has been destroyed.

issues.definition: A civil court has jurisdiction when a landlord sues for possession of vacant land, the rented building has been completely destroyed with no superstructure remaining, and the applicable rent-control scheme neither covers vacant land nor provides a remedy to recover it.
